properties.natural_language: Any call to the MODEXP precompile (address 0x05) must have its length_of_BASE, length_of_EXPONENT, and length_of_MODULUS parameters each validated to be <= 1024 bytes before computation proceeds.
The input data buffer provided to the MODEXP precompile must be parseable into three length parameters (length_of_BASE, length_of_EXPONENT, length_of_MODULUS) before any length validation occurs.
If any MODEXP length parameter exceeds 1024 bytes, the precompile must consume all gas allocated to the call and return an error status.
If all MODEXP length parameters are within the 1024-byte limit, the precompile must proceed with standard MODEXP computation per EIP-198.
The length check for MODEXP inputs must occur before any complex pricing calculation or modular exponentiation computation begins.
All client implementations must implement the MODEXP 1024-byte bounds check identically to prevent consensus failures.
An attacker submitting input with length parameters exceeding 1024 bytes must have the input immediately rejected without complex processing.
Post-EIP7823, the MODEXP input domain is finite and bounded (each parameter <= 8192 bits), enabling exhaustive testing.
When a MODEXP input violation is detected, all gas allocated to the call must be consumed before returning an error, economically penalizing the caller.
Before any Whisper envelope exchange can occur, both peers must have completed a status message (0x00) handshake including version, PoW requirement, and optional bloom filter.
Any message envelope received from a peer must be validated for correct structure [Expiry(4), TTL(4), Topic(4), Data(var), Nonce(8)] before acceptance.
Envelope Proof-of-Work must be validated as a valid numeric value (not NaN, INF, or negative) and must meet the minimum PoW requirement before the envelope is accepted.
After an envelope fails validation, it must be silently dropped without notifying the sender, unless the failure constitutes a severe protocol violation warranting peer disconnection.
Unknown packet codes must be silently ignored, while malformed packets (invalid encoding) must be rejected.
The bloom filter used for topic filtering must use at most 3 bits per bloomed topic within a 512-bit space.
Messages submitted by an application must be encrypted using either ECIES (asymmetric) or AES-GCM (symmetric) before being wrapped in an envelope for transmission.
After encryption and signing, 256-byte alignment padding must be applied to the message to prevent size-based metadata leakage.
Whisper message confidentiality relies on ECIES/AES-GCM not being broken within the message TTL timeframe; if encryption is broken, all message privacy is compromised.
Sufficient network peers must exist to provide anonymity through message mixing; with few peers, message origin could be determined through timing analysis.
A builder must submit a valid SignedExecutionPayloadHeader containing a bid value and blockhash commitment before a proposer can select it for inclusion.
The builder's BLS signature on the execution payload header must be verified as valid before the proposer includes it in the beacon block.
After a builder's commitment is included in a beacon block, the builder's beacon chain balance must be debited by the bid value, creating a BuilderPendingPayment.
The proposer must receive the builder's bid payment unconditionally, regardless of whether the builder subsequently reveals the execution payload.
A PTC attestation message must come from a validator assigned to the PTC for the current slot (one of 512 validators) and must indicate payload_present and blob_data_available status.
A slot is marked as FULL (payload included) only if at least 256 of 512 PTC members attest that the payload is present and blob data is available.
If the PTC threshold of 256 votes is not met or the payload is absent, the slot must be marked as EMPTY (payload withheld).

The execution payload envelope received from the builder must pass signature verification, blockhash matching, execution state transition validation, withdrawals root match, and beacon state root match before acceptance.
If any validation check fails (signature, blockhash, execution, withdrawals, state root), the envelope must be rejected and not included in the chain.
The blob_data_available boolean requires ALL blobs referenced in the commitment to be available; partial availability must be treated as unavailable.
BuilderPendingPayment is only created if the beacon block containing the commitment is accepted into the chain; rejected blocks must not create payments.
After epoch processing, BuilderPendingPayments must be converted to BuilderPendingWithdrawals and ultimately credited to the builder's fee_recipient on the execution layer.
A builder must have sufficient beacon chain validator balance exceeding the bid value before the balance deduction can occur.
An attacker controlling 35% of total stake requires approximately 205,000 years to gain majority control of the PTC; if PTC can be controlled more cheaply, payload censorship becomes feasible.
Builder equivocation (broadcasting conflicting payloads for the same slot) must not lead to slashing, but may result in split PTC views degrading consensus quality.
Colluding proposers controlling consecutive slots with >20% total stake could potentially reorg a builder's payload while keeping the payment; this is an accepted attack surface.
Before contract deployment via CREATE, CREATE2, or creation transaction, the target address must be checked for existing state: nonce must equal 0 AND code length must equal 0.

If a collision is detected (nonce > 0 OR code length > 0 at target address), the creation must be treated as an invalid opcode: all gas consumed, state changes reverted, zero address returned to caller.
If the target address has nonce == 0 AND code length == 0, the address is available and contract deployment must proceed.
Deployed contract code is immutable: once code exists at an address, no new deployment can overwrite it via address collision.
The collision check must happen against the pre-creation state; the nonce at the target address before any modifications from the current transaction must be zero.
Balance alone at a target address does not trigger collision detection; only nonce > 0 OR code.length > 0 causes creation failure.

Computing an address collision with an existing contract requires computational resources comparable to a Keccak-256 preimage attack; if this becomes feasible, CREATE2 collision attacks become possible.
All Ethereum clients must implement the collision check identically and atomically to prevent consensus failures.
The consensus layer must provide a valid parent_beacon_block_root in the execution block header before block processing begins.
After the system call to the beacon roots contract, the block timestamp must be stored at index (timestamp % 8191) and the beacon root must be stored at index (timestamp % 8191) + 8191.
A query to the beacon roots contract must provide exactly 32 bytes of non-zero input representing a timestamp.
After a valid query, the stored timestamp at the computed index must match the queried timestamp; if they do not match (stale/missing data), the query must revert.
If the timestamp matches, the beacon root stored at (index + HISTORY_BUFFER_LENGTH) must be returned to the caller.
The execution layer unconditionally trusts beacon block roots from the consensus layer without independent verification; CL compromise implies EL compromise.
Block timestamps must be monotonically increasing; timestamp manipulation could cause ring buffer collisions allowing overwrite of recent beacon roots with stale ones.
The system call to the beacon roots contract is allocated 30,000,000 gas that is NOT deducted from the block gas limit, and executes with value=0 and no EIP-1559 burn semantics.
If no code exists at the beacon roots contract address, the system call must fail silently and block processing must continue normally.
Queries for timestamps before the fork activation (FORK_TIMESTAMP) will fail timestamp match validation since no beacon root data was stored before activation.
All Dencun execution layer changes (EIP-1153, EIP-4844, EIP-5656, EIP-6780, EIP-7516) must be applied atomically at the fork block boundary.
All Dencun consensus layer changes (EIP-4788, EIP-7044, EIP-7045, EIP-7514) must be applied atomically at the fork epoch boundary.
The Dencun fork transition must only occur when the current epoch equals or exceeds the configured activation epoch (269568 for mainnet).
All client implementations must have updated to support Dencun before the activation epoch; non-upgraded nodes will fork off the canonical chain.
Execution layer timestamp-based activation and consensus layer epoch-based activation must be coordinated such that the first slot of the activation epoch corresponds to the expected fork timestamp.
SELFDESTRUCT and SUICIDE are aliases for the same opcode 0xFF; both keywords must produce identical bytecode and identical EVM behavior.
After SELFDESTRUCT/SUICIDE executes, the contract must be marked for deletion and all remaining ETH balance must be transferred to the designated beneficiary address.

Existing contracts compiled with the 'suicide' keyword must continue to function identically after EIP-6 adoption; the aliasing is purely at the compiler/documentation level, not at the EVM bytecode level.
The eth_symbol JSON-RPC request must take no parameters and return a string representing the native currency symbol.
The eth_symbol response must be a valid JSON-RPC response with a string result before the client accepts it for display.
There is no on-chain mechanism to verify the correctness of the symbol returned by eth_symbol; the client must trust the node operator or cross-reference with chain ID.
A malicious RPC node can return any symbol string, potentially deceiving users about which network they are connected to; wallets should cross-reference with chain ID.
The eth_symbol endpoint is read-only and informational with no consensus implications; it cannot affect on-chain state.
The symbol response should follow typical conventions of 2-5 uppercase ASCII characters; applications must sanitize display to prevent injection attacks.
The maximum gas refund for any transaction is capped at gas_used / MAX_REFUND_QUOTIENT where MAX_REFUND_QUOTIENT = 5, meaning at most 20% of gas used can be refunded.
After refund calculation, the actual refund applied to the sender must equal min(accumulated_refund_counter, gas_used / 5).
When a storage slot transitions from nonzero to zero (clearing), exactly 4800 gas (SSTORE_RESET_GAS + ACCESS_LIST_STORAGE_KEY_COST) must be added to the refund counter.
When a storage slot transitions zero → nonzero → zero in the same transaction, exactly 19900 gas must be added to the refund counter.
When a storage slot value is reverted to its original value (new == original && current != original), exactly 4900 gas must be added to the refund counter.
SELFDESTRUCT operations must NOT add any gas refund to the refund counter; the previous 24000 gas refund for SELFDESTRUCT is removed.
With the 20% refund cap, the maximum effective gas used per block is bounded to 125% of the block gas limit (1.25x), limiting state growth from storage operations.
The EIP-2929/2930 access list costs used in SSTORE_CLEARS_SCHEDULE calculation must be correctly integrated with the refund values.
A silent signing permission request must specify chain ID, contract address, function signatures, and expiry timestamp before the wallet displays a consent prompt.
The permission request must pass all validation checks: valid chain ID, valid contract address format, valid function signatures (4-byte selectors), and future expiry timestamp.
After user grants permission, the wallet must generate a cryptographically secure permissionSecret token and return it to the application.
Before a silent transaction is signed, the permissionSecret must be verified as valid and not expired, AND the transaction must target a permitted contract and function.
If permissionSecret is invalid/expired OR transaction is out of scope, the transaction must be rejected without signing.
After all checks pass, the wallet must sign the transaction without user interaction and broadcast it to the blockchain network.
Silent signing permissions must be time-bounded: once the unix timestamp exceeds the 'until' parameter, the permission must become invalid and all subsequent signing attempts must be rejected.
Users must be able to manually revoke silent signing permissions at any time before expiry, immediately invalidating the permissionSecret.
The wallet must display the full permission scope (contract, functions, duration) to the user before they can grant consent; the user must be able to make an informed decision.
Both temporal bounds and scope bounds must be enforced on every silent signing attempt; bypassing either boundary must result in transaction rejection.
If the permissionSecret is stolen by an attacker, they can submit transactions within the granted scope until the permission expires; the secret must have at least 128 bits of entropy.
Function scope restriction must distinguish overloaded functions by their 4-byte selector derived from the full signature, not by function name alone.
